chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from al-Abbas, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from Isma'il ibn 'Abbad, from Khirash, from some of our companions, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I said to him, 'May I be your ransom, indeed these opponents of ours say: When the sky is completely overcast or darkened so that we do not recognize the direction of the sky, we and you are equal in ijtihad (deduction).' He said, 'It is not as they say. If that is the case, let him pray facing four directions.'

key_terms.الْمُخَالِفِينَ: Opponents (referring to other Islamic sects or schools)
key_terms.لِأَرْعِ وُجُوهٍ: Facing four directions (a specific ruling for obscured Qibla)

ai.seo_question: How should one perform prayer when the sky is completely dark or overcast and the Qibla cannot be seen?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) refutes the claim that laypeople and scholars are equal in *ijtihad* when the Qibla is obscured by darkness, ruling that one should pray facing four directions. This ruling highlights the principle of *istishab* (presumption of continuity) and the obligation to do one's utmost (*wujub al-kifayah*) in prayer, distinguishing the scholarly duty of precise deduction from the practical concession for the general public. It underscores the Shia jurisprudential view that while scholars strive for accuracy, the validity of prayer for all remains secure through this comprehensive directional coverage.
